How to read a degree audit and compare what-if plans

A degree audit shows how learning fits a particular set of graduation requirements. A what-if plan asks how the same learning would fit a different degree, major, or school. Keep the original records fixed while comparing their possible placements.

Compare my degree options

Begin with the exact requirements

Find the current program requirements and establish which catalog applies to you. Capture the school, degree, major or concentration, minor if any, and attendance format. If a school has already issued your audit, use it as the starting point and ask about anything you do not understand.

An unofficial worksheet can help you prepare, but it should not claim to be the school’s award decision. Likewise, a degree plan shared online may describe a different catalog or student. Copy its structure and useful questions, then reconcile its requirements against your own destination.

Read the requirement row before the course name

For each row, ask what is required: a named course, a subject distribution, upper-level work, an elective block, or a university-only requirement. Record the needed credits and any minimum grade, prerequisite, or other condition. Then list the completed or proposed learning that might meet it.

This avoids a common mistake: seeing a familiar course title and assuming it fills the featured university course. A school may award an elective instead. A category substitution may be valid without being an exact course equivalency. Use the award the school actually identifies, and leave a question where that evidence is missing.

Keep status and evidence separate

A planned course has not been earned. A completed course may still be waiting for evaluation. A school-confirmed placement means the destination has applied that learning to the identified requirement. Those are different states even when they appear in the same row.

Save the supporting record, date, and program scope with each confirmation. If you change the source identity or switch to another degree, do not carry the old confirmation over automatically. A student report about another person’s outcome can inform a question without becoming your individual evaluation.

Count each source once

A three-credit source should not become six unique credits because it appears in two places on a worksheet. Some programs permit a course to satisfy more than one condition, but overlapping conditions do not necessarily create extra credit hours. Ask the school how permitted overlap affects the total.

Also check bundles and similar learning. A certificate might contain several recommended subjects, some of which duplicate previous courses. Keep the original source amount and its allocations visible. Extra accepted electives can remain in your inventory even when they do not reduce your remaining degree requirements.

Change one decision at a time

For a useful what-if comparison, save your current route and change the target or a small set of choices. Reapply the same inventory to each degree. Compare the actual university work left, uncertain matches, source restrictions, upper-level requirements, prerequisites, and costs still missing.

For example, changing a major might make a completed statistics course useful in the core while leaving a writing course in electives. It could also introduce a new prerequisite sequence. The better route is not necessarily the one with the highest total of accepted credits; it may be the route with fewer blocking requirements or a better fit for your career.

Take a short decision list to the school

Ask the transfer or advising team to resolve the rows with the largest consequences first. Include exact outside course identifiers and catalog details. When appealing a placement, ask what syllabus, assessment description, or other documentation the evaluator needs rather than assuming a title match proves the case.

End your comparison with the next three actions: collect a missing record, confirm an uncertain placement, or check a required course’s schedule. Update the ledger when the answer arrives. Keep the full course spreadsheet for detail and a short summary for decisions, so the plan remains understandable as it becomes more accurate.

About this research

DegreeSteps editorial team · Degree planning and transfer-credit research

We explain educational choices using university catalogs, receiving-school course agreements, provider guidance, and the same researched degree models used by DegreeSteps.
